setup: Altman Z-score, $Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 0.999X_5$. A firm has total assets 670,000, working capital 170,000, retained earnings 300,000, EBIT 60,000, market equity 380,000, total liabilities 240,000 and sales 2,200,000.
ask: Which is bigger: the $0.999X_5$ (sales/assets) term alone, or the other four terms combined?

options.label: The other four combined
options.why: The four together come to only about 2.18. Sales are 3.3× total assets, so $X_5 \approx 3.28$ on its own outweighs them.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 3.28 versus 2.18 is a 50% gap. Asset turnover (3.28) is by far the largest ratio, and its weight of 0.999 barely shrinks it.

takeaway: For a high-turnover firm, X5 (sales/assets) can carry most of the Z-score. Check it first.

setup: S&P cumulative default rates for a **B**-rated issuer: 3.34% by year 1, 7.80% by year 2, 11.75% by year 3. The cumulative figure keeps climbing.
ask: Is the marginal (unconditional) PD in year 3 larger or smaller than in year 2?

options.label: Larger in year 3
options.why: A rising cumulative PD tells you nothing about whether the yearly increments are rising. Year 2 adds 4.46 points and year 3 adds only 3.95.

options.label: Equal
options.why: The increments are 4.46 and 3.95. They differ by about half a point, so they are not equal.

working.label: Comparison
working.display: $3.95\% < 4.46\%$: the B-rated marginal profile peaks in year 2 and then falls

takeaway: Speculative-grade marginal PDs peak early and then decline once the issuer survives. Investment-grade marginal PDs tend to rise over time.

setup: Constant hazard rate $\lambda = 2\%$. Cumulative PD is $1 - e^{-0.02 \times 4} = 7.69\%$ by year 4 and $1 - e^{-0.02 \times 5} = 9.52\%$ by year 5. So the unconditional PD during year 5 is $1.83\%$.
ask: The PD in year 5 *conditional on surviving to year 4*: higher than, lower than, or equal to 1.83%?

options.label: Lower than 1.83%
options.why: Conditioning divides by the survival probability $1 - 0.0769 < 1$, which can only make the number larger.

options.label: Equal to 1.83%
options.why: The two coincide only in year 1, when survival to the start of the year is 100%. By year 5 the survival factor is 92.3%.

takeaway: Conditional PD = marginal / survival, so it is always at least as large as the unconditional PD. Under a constant hazard it stays flat at 1 − e^(−λ).

setup: CDS spreads: 5-year 90 bp, 10-year 110 bp. Expected recovery is 65%. Average hazard rates are bootstrapped with $\bar\lambda = s/(1-RR)$.
ask: The average hazard rate between year 5 and year 10 is closest to?

options.why: You bootstrapped the raw spreads, $(10 \times 1.10\% - 5 \times 0.90\%)/5$, without dividing by $LGD = 0.35$.
You forgot to divide the time-weighted difference $10\bar\lambda_{10} - 5\bar\lambda_5 = 0.186$ by the 5-year span.
Scale slip (0.1×), e.g. a decimal slip when converting bp to percent.

takeaway: Forward hazard = time-weighted difference of cumulative averages, divided by the gap in years. Gross spreads up by LGD first.

setup: 5-year iTraxx Europe is quoted bid 150 bp / ask 152 bp. The index has 125 names. An investor buys EUR 500,000 of protection on *each* name.
ask: The annual premium paid is closest to?

options.label: ≈ EUR 7,600
options.why: That is the premium for one name ($0.0152 \times 500{,}000$). You forgot the ×125. It is also the amount the annual payments fall by after one default.

options.label: ≈ EUR 95,000
options.why: You read 152 bp as 0.152% instead of 1.52%, a bp-to-decimal slip.

options.label: ≈ EUR 95m
options.why: You used 1.52 as a decimal (152%) instead of 0.0152.

working.label: Rate
working.display: Buyer of protection pays the ask: $152 \text{ bp} = 0.0152$

takeaway: Index premium = ask spread × notional per name × number of names. A protection buyer pays the ask.

setup: Merton model. Equity $E_0 = 3$, equity volatility $\sigma_E = 80\%$, solved firm value $V_0 = 12.40$, and equity delta $N(d_1) = 0.912$. Use $\sigma_E E_0 = N(d_1)\,\sigma_V V_0$.
ask: Asset volatility $\sigma_V$ is closest to?

options.why: That is the equity volatility. Equity is a levered claim, so $\sigma_V$ must be much lower than $\sigma_E$.
You inverted the leverage ratio: $\sigma_E \times V_0/E_0 = 0.8 \times 12.4/3$. Asset vol cannot exceed equity vol here.
Scale slip (0.3×).

takeaway: Asset vol = equity vol × (E/V) ÷ delta. With leverage it comes out far below equity vol.

setup: The CDS-bond basis is defined as $\text{CDS spread} - \text{bond yield spread}$. A CDS contract lets the protection buyer deliver the *cheapest-to-deliver* bond on default.
ask: This feature pushes the basis: positive, negative, or no effect?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Negative-basis drivers make CDS protection worth less than it looks: counterparty risk, accrued interest excluded from the payoff, bonds above par. The CTD option works the other way.

options.label: No effect
options.why: The CTD option has value to the protection buyer, and the seller charges for it in the spread.

working.label: Who holds the option
working.display: The protection buyer chooses what to deliver, which is an extra option

working.label: Effect
working.display: Protection is worth more → CDS spread rises relative to the bond spread → basis > 0

takeaway: Anything that hands the protection buyer an extra option (CTD, restructuring clause) pushes the basis positive.

setup: A counterparty's credit spread is 2%. The implied hazard rate is $\lambda = s/(1-RR)$. The desk revises its recovery assumption from 40% to 60%, with the spread unchanged.
ask: The implied hazard rate: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Intuition says 'better recovery, safer name', but the spread is fixed. A smaller LGD means a larger default probability is needed to explain the same spread.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The spread is unchanged, but it is divided by LGD. LGD moves from 0.60 to 0.40, so the ratio moves too.

working.label: CVA side
working.display: LGD falls from 60% to 40%. Per the reading, the LGD effect dominates, so CVA falls even though the implied PD rises

takeaway: Holding the spread fixed, higher recovery → higher implied PD but lower CVA.

setup: $EPE = 100$, $ENE = -80$, both LGDs 60%, counterparty $PD_C = 2\%$, own $PD_I = 1.5\%$. You have computed $CVA = -0.6(100)(0.02) = -1.20$. Next comes $DVA = -LGD_I \times ENE \times PD_I$, and then $BCVA = CVA + DVA$.
ask: Compared with CVA alone (−1.20), is BCVA more negative, less negative, or the same?

options.label: More negative
options.why: You treated DVA as another cost. With $ENE < 0$ the product $-LGD \times ENE \times PD$ is **positive**, so DVA is a benefit. Taking it as negative gives −1.92.

options.label: The same
options.why: That is unilateral CVA, which ignores your own default. BCVA admits both defaults, so the DVA term is switched on.

takeaway: ENE is negative, so DVA comes out positive. BCVA is less negative than UCVA.

setup: A swap with notional USD 100m and risky duration 3.75 carries a CVA of $-90{,}000$. The desk wants it as a running spread.
ask: The running spread is closest to?

options.label: ≈ −9.0 bp
options.why: You divided by notional only ($-90{,}000/100\text{m}$). The upfront CVA must also be spread over the risky duration.

options.label: ≈ −34 bp
options.why: You multiplied by the risky duration instead of dividing.

options.label: ≈ −0.24 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×), a bp conversion off by a factor of 10.

takeaway: Running spread = CVA ÷ (risky duration × notional). A negative CVA gives a negative spread, charged to the counterparty.

setup: You have a bilateral trade. Your exposure to the counterparty tends to *increase* as its credit quality *worsens* (wrong-way risk).
ask: Relative to the independence case, your DVA: increases, decreases, or unaffected?

options.label: Increases
options.why: That is the CVA effect: wrong-way risk increases CVA. DVA moves the opposite way. The same correlation reduces DVA.

options.label: Unaffected
options.why: CVA and DVA are driven by the same exposure paths. A dependence between exposure and default changes both.

working.label: Wrong-way risk
working.display: Positive correlation between your exposure and the counterparty's default probability

working.label: Directions
working.display: CVA ↑ (cost grows), DVA ↓ (benefit shrinks). Right-way risk flips both

takeaway: Wrong-way risk: CVA up, DVA down. Right-way risk: CVA down, DVA up.

setup: A securitization has equity, mezzanine and senior tranches. Default probabilities are held fixed while the default correlation across the loan pool increases.
ask: The value of the **equity** tranche: rises, falls, or depends on the default rate?

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is the senior tranche. Higher correlation makes the extreme pool-wide losses that reach a senior note more likely.

options.label: Depends on the default rate
options.why: That describes the mezzanine tranche, which flips: down at low default rates, up at high ones.

working.label: Low correlation
working.display: Defaults cluster near their expected value, so the equity writedown is near-certain

working.label: High correlation
working.display: Outcomes spread out, including more scenarios with zero or very few defaults. That upside goes to equity

takeaway: Correlation is a bet on dispersion: equity is long it, senior is short it, and mezzanine flips.

setup: A CLO has 100 loans of USD 1m at 8.5%. Bond coupons due are USD 5,675,000 a year. Up to USD 1,750,000 of excess spread a year goes to the OC account and the rest goes to equity. 5% of surviving loans default each year, paying no interest, and are not replaced. 95 loans survived year 1.
ask: Cash paid to equity in year 2 is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.65m
options.why: That is year 1's figure. You forgot that 4.75 more loans default in year 2, leaving 90.25 paying interest.

options.label: ≈ USD 2.0m
options.why: That is the full year-2 excess spread. You skipped the USD 1.75m diversion to the overcollateralization account.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.074m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

takeaway: Equity gets only what excess spread leaves above the OC cap, and each year's defaults shrink the base.

setup: Same CLO. Year 1: 95 loans paid 8.5% on USD 1m each, excess spread was USD 2,400,000, and equity got USD 650,000 after the USD 1,750,000 OC diversion. Year 2: 4.75 more loans default. Bond coupons due stay at USD 5,675,000.
ask: In year 2, how does the excess spread compare with the USD 1.75m cap?

options.label: Above the cap: equity still gets a small residual
Below the cap: all of it goes to the OC account
options.why: Excess spread falls but is still about USD 2.0m: $90.25 \times 85{,}000 - 5{,}675{,}000$. It is USD 246k above the cap.

options.label: Negative: the OC account pays the shortfall
options.why: Excess spread turns negative only once fewer than $5{,}675{,}000/85{,}000 = 66.8$ loans survive. There are 90.25 here.

takeaway: Two custodian tests each year: is excess spread > 0, and is it > the cap K? Equity is paid only if both are yes.

setup: Same CLO, same 5% annual default rate on surviving loans. At the start of year 5, $100 \times 0.95^4 = 81.45$ loans survive, each USD 1m at 8.5%; loans that default during year 5 pay no interest that year. Bond coupons due are USD 5,675,000 and the OC cap is USD 1,750,000.
ask: Year-5 excess spread is:

options.label: Positive but below the cap: all of it goes to OC, equity gets nothing
Above the cap: equity gets the residual
options.why: About 77.4 loans pay interest, giving USD 6.58m. That leaves only about USD 0.90m of excess spread, well short of the USD 1.75m cap.

options.label: Negative: the OC account pays the shortfall
options.why: Negative only below $5{,}675{,}000/85{,}000 = 66.8$ surviving loans. At 77.4 the structure still covers its coupons.

working.label: vs cap
working.display: $902{,}150 < 1{,}750{,}000$ → all diverted to OC, equity gets 0

takeaway: Excess spread shrinks with the pool. Equity cash dries up well before the structure fails to cover coupons.

setup: Next week a bank expects USD 150m of new qualifying loan requests and a USD 75m Treasury purchase. It also expects USD 135m of drawings on existing credit lines. You've already totalled sources: USD 185m received today plus USD 100m expected = USD 285m.
ask: The available funds gap: a shortfall (positive), a surplus (negative), or about zero?

options.label: A surplus
options.why: You dropped the credit-line drawings: $150 + 75 - 285 = -60$. Drawings on committed lines are a use of funds.

options.label: About zero
options.why: You dropped the securities purchase: $150 + 135 - 285 = 0$. Planned investments are a use too.

takeaway: AFG = (loans + investments + expected line drawings) − (current + expected inflows). Positive means a shortfall.

setup: Historical average cost approach. Total funds raised USD 1,000m, total interest paid USD 65m, other operating costs USD 10m, earning assets USD 750m.
ask: Which is bigger: the weighted average interest expense (step 1) or the break-even cost rate on earning assets (step 2)?

options.label: The weighted interest expense
options.why: Step 2 adds USD 10m of operating costs to the numerator and divides by the smaller earning-asset base. Both push it up.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Even with the wrong USD 1,000m denominator, step 2 would be 7.5%. With the correct USD 750m it is 10%, well above 6.5%.

takeaway: The denominator switches from total funds (step 1) to earning assets (steps 2–3). 6.5%, 10% and 12.46% are all correct answers to different questions.

setup: Pooled-funds approach. New funds: USD 100m transaction deposits (50% placeable), USD 100m time deposits (60% placeable) and USD 100m new equity (90% placeable). Total operating cost is USD 30m. Suppose the time-deposit placeable share drops to 40%, with costs unchanged.
ask: The hurdle rate on earning assets: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: A smaller placeable base cannot lower the hurdle. The same USD 30m must be recovered from fewer earning dollars.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The pooled funds *expense* (30/300 = 10%) is unchanged. The hurdle, though, divides by dollars placeable, which fall from 200 to 180.

takeaway: Pooled-funds hurdle = operating costs ÷ dollars placeable in earning assets. Less placeable money means a higher hurdle.

setup: A repo: bonds with face USD 10m and market value USD 11m are sold for USD 11m and repurchased after 31 days. The repo rate is 0.3% (actual/360), with no haircut or accrued interest.
ask: The repo interest (settlement minus USD 11m) is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 33,000
options.why: You applied the annual rate for a full year ($0.003 \times 11\text{m}$) and forgot the $31/360$ day fraction.

options.label: ≈ USD 280,000
options.why: You used 0.3 (30%) instead of 0.003, a percent-to-decimal slip.

options.label: ≈ USD 280
options.why: You read 0.3% as 0.03%, a slip by a factor of 10.

working.label: Contract price
working.display: USD 11m market value (not the USD 10m face)

takeaway: Repo settlement = contract price × (1 + rate × days/360), on market value. At 0.3% a month's interest is tiny.

setup: The OTR 10-year trades special: the special spread is 0.22% for 125 days (actual/360). Price is 101.90 and DV01 is 0.085 per 100 face.
ask: The financing advantage, in yield terms, is closest to?

options.label: ≈ 92 bp
options.why: You used 0.22 as the decimal spread instead of 0.0022.

options.label: ≈ 0.0066 bp
options.why: You multiplied the dollar value by DV01 instead of dividing. Dollar value ÷ DV01 gives basis points.

options.label: ≈ 9 bp
options.why: Scale slip (10×).

takeaway: Financing value: spread × days/360 → scale by price/100 → divide by DV01. It comes out at under a basis point.

setup: The OTR 10-year trades about 2.00 per 100 face rich to the C-STRIPS curve. You've valued its financing advantage (lending it at the special rate for 125 days) at 7.7 cents per 100 face.
ask: The rest of the premium (richness minus financing), attributed to liquidity: bigger or smaller than the financing value?

options.label: Much bigger: richness is mostly liquidity
Smaller: richness is mostly financing
options.why: 7.7 cents out of about 2 dollars is under 4%. Specialness explains only a sliver of OTR richness.

options.label: About the same
options.why: About 1.92 of liquidity against 0.077 of financing is a ratio of roughly 25 to 1.

takeaway: OTR premium = liquidity advantage + financing advantage, and the liquidity part is usually by far the larger.

setup: Since 2009 a failed delivery of a Treasury incurs a penalty rate of $\max(3\% - \text{FFR},\, 0)$. The fed funds rate rises from 1% to 2%.
ask: The penalty rate, and so the cap on the special spread: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: The penalty moves inversely with the fed funds rate. It is largest (3%) when rates are zero.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The 0 floor binds only once FFR ≥ 3%. At 1–2% the penalty is still falling one-for-one with FFR.

takeaway: Fails penalty = max(3% − FFR, 0): high rates mean a low penalty, and zero rates mean the full 3%.

setup: Special spread = GC repo rate − special repo rate for the on-the-run Treasury. Compare the days just before the next auction with the days just after it.
ask: Just before the auction, the OTR special spread is: wider, narrower, or the same?

options.label: Narrower
options.why: Right after an auction the new OTR issue is in surplus supply, which narrows specialness. Before the auction, demand for the scarce issue pushes it wider.

options.label: The same
options.why: Special spreads follow a systematic auction-cycle pattern; they are not flat.

working.label: After auction
working.display: New supply of the OTR issue → less scarce as collateral → special rate nearer GC → narrower

working.label: Before auction
working.display: Rising demand for the issue to borrow → special rate falls further below GC → wider

takeaway: OTR special spreads: wide before an auction, narrow just after (new supply).
